idiom_name: typedef'd opaque struct + create/destroy pair; static helpers with internal linkage
implementation_notes: C has neither classes nor access control, so the standalone boundary is hand-written: forward-declare the struct in the header (`typedef struct money Money;`) and define it only in the .c file, so callers can hold pointers but cannot see or alter the representation; give helpers `static` linkage so they never leave the translation unit that owns the type. What a reader of the public header sees is the type name plus functions over primitives and pointers to the type itself, which is the C equivalent of a class fully explained by its own definition. There is no library substitute - a hand-written handle is the classic form - and the alternative (a transparent struct) is worth taking when value semantics and stack allocation matter more than hiding the layout.
pitfalls: Because the header only forward-declares the struct, clients cannot allocate it on the stack or embed it in another struct: every instance needs the create/destroy pair, and a forgotten free leaks.
`typedef struct money *Money;` hides the pointer and makes const-correctness (`const Money *` versus a const pointer) unreadable - keep the `*` visible at the use site.

Nothing prevents another module from re-declaring the struct; once the layout is published in a shared private header the encapsulation is gone, so keep the public header free of the definition and share internals through `<module>_private.h`.
C has no overloading and no namespaces: every function must carry the type prefix (`money_plus`), so the API grows by convention rather than by structure.

variants.name: Transparent struct with free functions (value semantics)
variants.idiom_name: public struct definition + free functions over it, passed by value or by pointer to const
variants.implementation_notes: The opposite trade, and often the better one in C: publish the struct's layout in the header and pass it by value or by pointer, keeping only behaviour - not representation - behind the API. The pattern's goal is still met, because the reader can see the complete state of the type in its own definition without opening any other file, and no other model type appears in the functions' signatures; what is given up is the freedom to change the layout later without recompiling callers. Prefer it for small self-contained values in embedded or ABI-critical code, where an opaque handle's allocation and lifetime rules cost more than encapsulation buys.
pitfalls: Publishing the layout makes every field part of the API: adding or reordering members breaks the ABI and any caller using designated initialisers.
With the representation visible, invariants can be broken by direct field writes, so validation has to be repeated at each entry point - or the type is honestly just a record.
Passing the struct by value copies it; anything larger than a few words should be passed as a pointer to const to keep call sites cheap and intention-revealing.
